posts.title: 3 things that shape a Charleston custom home

instagram.caption:
3 things that shape a Charleston custom home before a single board goes up: 👉

1️⃣ Elevation. The City of Charleston requires new homes to be built 2 feet above FEMA's flood standard. That affects the foundation, the steps, the porch and how the house sits on the street.

2️⃣ Review. In the historic districts, the Board of Architectural Review has to approve the design before construction starts. Plan for that step from the beginning.

3️⃣ Salt and wind. Stainless fasteners, impact-rated windows and materials that hold up to coastal air cost more upfront. They also mean you aren't replacing things in five years.

That's why our process starts with a walk of the site and an honest budget conversation.

Ready to start? DM us "BUILD."

Sources: City of Charleston flood ordinance (2 ft freeboard, effective July 1, 2020); City of Charleston Board of Architectural Review.

facebook.caption:
What shapes a Charleston custom home before the first board goes up? Usually three things.

Elevation. The City of Charleston requires new construction to be built 2 feet above FEMA's flood standard. That one rule affects the foundation, the entry, the porch and how the home looks from the street.

Architectural review. In the historic districts, the Board of Architectural Review approves the design before construction starts. It's part of what keeps Charleston looking like Charleston, and it needs to be built into the timeline from the beginning.

Coastal materials. Salt air and hurricane-season wind are hard on a house. Stainless fasteners, impact-rated windows and durable exterior materials cost more upfront. They cost far less than replacing things later.

That's why our process starts before design: a walk of the site, a budget consultation, a realistic price range, and then the right architect and designer for the project.

Thinking about building? Start here: https://renewurban.net/contact/

Sources: City of Charleston flood ordinance (effective July 1, 2020); City of Charleston Board of Architectural Review.
